meta.grounding: Synthesized by Claude from the five processed feeds. Every figure traces to primary NYC data; interpretation is the model's and clearly hedged.

headline: Filings up 24% in July 2026 while May 2026 sales fall 15%; citywide ownership requires 2.4x the median income
summary: Development filings reached 1,536 in July 2026 (74,533 units), up 24% year-over-year and 15% above baseline, while recorded sales in May 2026 fell 15% year-over-year to 3,921 even as the median price rose 5% to $940,000. Financing benchmarks are mixed as of August 4, 2026: the 10-Year Treasury is 4.63% (+40 bps year-over-year) while SOFR is 3.66% (-69 bps) and the 30-Year Mortgage is 6.66% (-18 bps). Against ACS 5-year 2024 incomes, buying the citywide median home requires $193,302 versus a median household income of $80,483 — a 2.4x gap, with 19% estimated able to afford and 52% of renters cost-burdened.

insights.title: Supply expanding while recorded demand contracts
insights.detail: July 2026 filings rose 24% year-over-year citywide (1,536 filings, 74,533 units), with Manhattan +58% (109 filings), Brooklyn +33% (493) and Staten Island +30% (195) flagged Elevated. May 2026 sales moved the other way: -15% citywide, with Queens -27% (1,116 sales) and Staten Island -28% (249) classified Cooling. DATA notes filings are not rate-driven (DOB NOW migration and policy deadlines), so the two series should be read as separate signals rather than one causing the other.

insights.title: Cost-of-capital context is mixed, and the sales link is an association only
insights.detail: As of August 4, 2026: 10-Year Treasury 4.63% (+40 bps year-over-year), 30-Year Mortgage 6.66% (-18 bps), SOFR 3.66% (-69 bps), Fed Funds 3.63% (-70 bps). Versus the 2021 low-rate boom, mortgage rates moved from 2.96% to 6.36% and recorded sales from 5,902 to 4,358 per month (-26%) over June 2025–May 2026. The year-over-year mortgage-vs-sales correlation is -0.21, which DATA labels association, not causation.

insights.title: Price gains outpace measured purchasing power
insights.detail: The May 2026 citywide median price of $940,000 is up 5% year-over-year, while the ACS 5-year 2024 read shows $193,302 of income required to buy against $80,483 median household income (2.4x gap, 19% share able to afford). Over the 2020→2024 window, incomes grew 20% while rents grew 22% and home values 22%. These are different periods — the affordability read is structural, annual and lagged — so the comparison frames context rather than explaining the May 2026 move; the 52% renter cost-burden figure is worth watching alongside it.

insights.title: Oversupply-watch ZIPs pair rising filings with falling sales and hazardous violations
insights.detail: Over March 2026–May 2026, Schuylerville/Pelham Bay (10461) shows supply +190% against demand -18% with 386 immediately hazardous violations; Ocean Parkway-North (11218) +144% supply, -26% demand, 495 violations; Flatbush-East (11203) +100% supply, -18% demand, 973 violations; Bay Ridge (11209) +67% supply, -47% demand, 388 violations. The combination of added pipeline, softer recorded demand and existing-stock violations suggests these submarkets merit closer diligence.

insights.title: Local Law 97: 73% of covered buildings above the 2030 limit
insights.detail: For report year 2024, 28,925 covered buildings show 18% over the 2024 limit and 73% over the 2030 limit, with estimated annual penalty exposure of $759M (2024) rising to $2,282M (2030). Manhattan accounts for $381M of estimated penalty with 75% over the 2030 limit; the Bronx shows $142M and 78% over 2030. Compliance timelines are a fixed deadline rather than a market-cycle variable.

neighborhoods.narrative: May 2026 sales of 1,116 were down 27% year-over-year at a $778,500 median, a Cooling regime, while July 2026 filings of 398 were up 9% and In range. On affordability (ACS 5-year 2024), Queens requires $160,091 to buy versus $86,136 median income — a 1.86x gap with 23% able to afford, classified Supported growth. Risk pressure of 29,890 was flat year-over-year (0%) with 6,487 Class C violations.

Filings rose 58% to 109 in July 2026 (Elevated), while May 2026 sales of 1,184 were down only 2% at a $1,440,000 median (In range). ACS 5-year 2024 affordability shows $296,122 income required versus $103,931 median income (2.85x, 13% able to afford, 48% renter cost burden), classified Affordability stress. Manhattan also carries $381M of estimated annual LL97 penalty exposure with 75% of covered buildings over the 2030 limit.

Filings of 341 were up 19% in July 2026 (In range); May 2026 sales of 323 fell 11% at a $700,000 median. Risk pressure of 108,062 rose 5% year-over-year with 23,033 Class C violations. Ownership economics are strained in low-income, majority-renter ZIPs: 10454 shows a 6.76x gap ($162,867 required vs. $24,086 median income) with 61% of renters cost-burdened, and 10453 a 4.18x gap with 65% cost-burdened — these are renter-cost signals, not evidence of broad local buying.

July 2026 filings of 195 were up 30% (Elevated) while May 2026 sales of 249 fell 28% at a $725,000 median (Cooling). Risk pressure of 5,286 rose 10% year-over-year with 1,094 Class C violations. Affordability (ACS 5-year 2024) shows a 1.52x gap ($149,089 required vs. $98,333 median income) and 31% able to afford, yet 57% of renters are cost-burdened and the borough is classed Affordability stress. Great Kills (10308) appears on the tightening list for March–May 2026 with supply -29% and demand +39%.

Filings of 493 were up 33% in July 2026 (Elevated); May 2026 sales of 1,049 fell 7% at a $1,075,000 median (In range). Canarsie (11236) appears on both lists: risk pressure of 1,242 up 61% year-over-year with 242 Class C violations, and supply +123% against demand -25% with 219 immediately hazardous violations over March–May 2026. Borough affordability is a 2.75x gap ($221,064 required vs. $80,263 median income), 14% able to afford, classified Supported growth.
